rules.rule: Give each frame one clear focal point, so the viewer's hierarchy of attention is never in doubt.
What is on screen supports the spoken line in hierarchy: it shows the claim being made, not a second one.
Keep on-screen text short enough for its legibility at the time it is held: a viewer reads it once, while listening.
Never trade legibility for fit: cut words before text falls below the pack's minimum size.
Use contrast to mean something: a change of colour, size or weight marks a change the viewer should notice.
Set the rhythm of cuts by the narration's sense units, not by a fixed interval.
Keep the rhythm slow enough that each shot holds until its text can be read.
Keep continuity: the same idea keeps the same position, colour and form across shots.
Use a transition other than a cut only when it carries continuity of meaning, such as time passing or a related idea.
For intelligibility, each scene argues one idea, and its shots serve that idea in order.
Prefer plain words for intelligibility: a term the brief does not define is explained or avoided.
